notes.front: What is a thermal switch fire detector?
notes.back: A heat-sensitive unit that completes an electrical circuit, lighting a warning light, at a certain temperature.
notes.explanation: The switches are wired in parallel with each other but in series with the indicator lights.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 9, “Thermal Switch System”, p. 9-2
notes.evidence: These thermal switches are heat-sensitive units that complete electrical circuits at a certain temperature. They are connected in parallel with each other, but in series with the indicator lights [Figure 9-1].
notes.example: Like a kettle’s thermostat, but closing a circuit to light a fire warning instead of switching off.

notes.front: What does thermocouple fire detection respond to?
notes.back: The rate of temperature rise.
notes.explanation: It gives no warning when an engine slowly overheats or a short circuit develops.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 9, “Thermocouple Systems”, p. 9-2
notes.evidence: The thermocouple fire warning system operates on an entirely different principle than the thermal switch system. A thermocouple depends on the rate of temperature rise and does not give a warning when an engine slowly overheats or a short circuit develops.
notes.example: Like a smoke alarm that reacts to a sudden change rather than a steady level, but sensing heat.

notes.front: What is a flame detector?
notes.back: An optical sensor that alarms when it detects the specific radiation emissions of hydrocarbon flames.
notes.explanation: The two types, infrared and ultraviolet, are named for the wavelengths they detect.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Airframe (FAA-H-8083-31B), ch. 17, “Flame Detectors”, p. 17-8
notes.evidence: Optical sensors, often referred to as flame detectors, are designed to alarm when they detect the presence of prominent, specific radiation emissions from hydrocarbon flames. The two types of optical sensors available are infrared (IR) and ultraviolet (UV), based on the specific emission wavelengths that they are designed to detect.
notes.example: Like an automatic door’s sensor, but watching for the light signature of a fuel fire.

notes.front: Where are infrared optical flame detectors mainly used?
notes.back: On light turboprop aircraft and helicopter engines.
notes.explanation: The handbook says they have proved very dependable and economical in these relatively benign environments.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 9, “Optical Fire Detection Systems”, p. 9-3
notes.evidence: IR-based optical flame detectors are used primarily on light turboprop aircraft and helicopter engines. These sensors have proven to be very dependable and economical for the relatively benign environments of these applications.
notes.example: Like a flame detector in a gas boiler, but watching a helicopter engine bay.

notes.front: What is a continuous-loop detector?
notes.back: A sensing system that covers a fire hazard area more completely than any spot-type temperature detector.
notes.explanation: Large commercial aircraft almost exclusively use such continuous thermal sensing elements for powerplant protection.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 9, “Continuous-Loop Detector Systems”, p. 9-3
notes.evidence: A continuous-loop detector, or sensing system, permits more complete coverage of a fire hazard area than any of the spot-type temperature detectors.
notes.example: Like a tripwire strung round a whole room instead of a few motion sensors in corners, but sensing heat.

notes.front: How does a pneumatic continuous-loop detector sense a fire?
notes.back: Heat raises the pressure of helium in a closed tube until a switch closes and signals an alarm.
notes.explanation: Pneumatic detectors are based on the gas laws.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 9, “Pneumatic Thermal Fire Detection”, p. 9-3
notes.evidence: Pneumatic detectors are based on the principles of gas laws. The sensing element consists of a closed helium-filled tube connected at one end to a responder assembly. As the element is heated, the gas pressure inside the tube increases until the alarm threshold is reached. At this point, an internal switch closes and reports an alarm to the flight deck.
notes.example: Like a sealed balloon whose pressure rises in the sun, but closing a switch when it gets hot enough.

notes.front: What is the Fenwal system’s sensing element made of?
notes.back: A slender Inconel tube packed with thermally sensitive eutectic salt around a nickel wire centre conductor.
notes.explanation: Lengths of these elements are connected in series to a control unit.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 9, “Fenwal Continuous-Loop System”, p. 9-3
notes.evidence: The Fenwal system uses a slender inconel tube packed with thermally sensitive eutectic salt and a nickel wire center
notes.example: Like an electric cable whose insulation turns conductive when hot, so heat anywhere along it is felt.

notes.front: What is the Kidde continuous-loop system’s sensing element?
notes.back: Two wires embedded in an Inconel tube filled with thermistor core material.
notes.explanation: One conductor is grounded to the tube and the other connects to the fire detection control unit.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 9, “Kidde Continuous-Loop System”, p. 9-4
notes.evidence: In the Kidde continuous-loop system, two wires are imbedded in an inconel tube filled with a thermistor core material. [Figure 9-5] Two electrical conductors go through the length of the core. One conductor has a ground connection to the tube and the other conductor connects to the fire detection control unit.
notes.example: Like the Fenwal element, but with two conductors and a thermistor core.

notes.front: What is dual-loop fire detection?
notes.back: Two complete fire detection systems whose outputs are connected so both must signal to give a fire warning.
notes.explanation: This “AND” logic greatly increases reliability against false fire warnings.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 9, “Dual-Loop Systems”, p. 9-6
notes.evidence: Dual-loop systems are, in essence, two complete basic fire detection systems with their output signals connected so that both must signal to result in a fire warning. This arrangement, called “AND” logic, results in greatly increased reliability against false fire warnings from any cause.
notes.example: Like a bank vault needing two keyholders to agree, but for fire warnings.

notes.front: How many discharges must the engine fire extinguishing system of a transport category aircraft certificated under part 25 provide?
notes.back: Two discharges, each producing adequate agent concentration.
notes.explanation: Commuter aircraft under part 23 need at minimum a one-shot system.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 9, “Engine Fire Extinguishing System”, p. 9-7
notes.evidence: Commuter aircraft certificated under 14 CFR part 23 are required to have, at a minimum, a one-shot fire extinguishing system. All transport category aircraft certificated under 14 CFR part 25 are required to have two discharges, each of which produces adequate agent concentration.
notes.example: Like a fire hose with a second, reserve supply behind it.

notes.front: What is Halon 1301?
notes.back: The most common engine fire extinguishing agent still used today.
notes.explanation: The handbook credits its effective firefighting capability and relatively low toxicity.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 9, “Fire Extinguishing Agents”, p. 9-7
notes.evidence: The most common extinguishing agent still used today is Halon 1301 because of its effective firefighting capability and relatively low toxicity (U.L. classification Group 61).
notes.example: Like the gas in a server-room fire system, but stored in engine fire bottles.

notes.front: What is a high rate of discharge (HRD) system?
notes.back: A system using open-end tubes to deliver a quantity of extinguishing agent in 1 to 2 seconds.
notes.explanation: Many other systems use perforated tubing or discharge nozzles to distribute the agent.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 9, “Fire Extinguishing Agents”, p. 9-7
notes.evidence: Many systems use perforated tubing or discharge nozzles to distribute the extinguishing agent. High rate of discharge (HRD) systems use open-end tubes to deliver a quantity of extinguishing agent in 1 to 2 seconds.
notes.example: Like emptying a bucket onto a fire instead of spraying it slowly from a hose.

notes.front: What does a fire extinguisher container (HRD bottle) hold?
notes.back: A liquid halogenated extinguishing agent and pressurised gas, typically nitrogen.
notes.explanation: Containers are normally made of stainless steel, with titanium among the alternatives.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 9, “Containers”, p. 9-8
notes.evidence: Fire extinguisher containers (HRD bottles) store a liquid halogenated extinguishing agent and pressurized gas (typically nitrogen) normally manufactured from stainless steel. Depending upon design considerations, alternate materials are available including titanium.
notes.example: Like an aerosol can, where a propellant gas pushes out the product, but holding extinguishing agent.

notes.front: What is fitted in the outlet of a fire extinguisher discharge valve assembly?
notes.back: A cartridge (squib) and a frangible disc type valve.
notes.explanation: Discharge valves are installed on the containers; some special assemblies use solenoid or manual seat valves.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 9, “Discharge Valves”, p. 9-8
notes.evidence: Discharge valves are installed on the containers. A cartridge (squib) and frangible disc type valve are installed in the outlet of the discharge valve assembly. Special assemblies having solenoid-operated or manually-operated seat type valves are also available.
notes.example: Like a champagne cork held in by a wire, but opened by a small explosive charge.

notes.front: What is a squib?
notes.back: An electrically operated explosive device in the container’s discharge assembly.
notes.explanation: When fired, it drives a slug through the breakable disc and nitrogen pressure pushes the Halon out.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 9, “Squib”, p. 9-16
notes.evidence: The squib is an electrically operated explosive device. When the squib is activated, it fires a slug through the breakable disc, and nitrogen pressure inside the bottle pushes the Halon through the discharge port.
notes.example: Like the charge that fires a car’s airbag, but opening a fire bottle.

notes.front: What is a two-way check valve in an engine fire extinguishing system for?
notes.back: In a two-shot system, it stops the reserve container’s agent backing up into the emptied main container.
notes.explanation: The handbook says these valves are required in a two-shot system.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 9, “Two-Way Check Valve”, p. 9-9
notes.evidence: These valves are required in a two-shot system to prevent the agent in a reserve container from backing up into the previous emptied main container.
notes.example: Like a one-way valve on a sink overflow, but keeping a reserve fire bottle from emptying into a spent one.

notes.front: What does a thermal discharge indicator (red disc) show?
notes.back: That the container’s contents have dumped overboard because of excessive heat.
notes.explanation: It is connected to the container relief fitting, and the agent leaves through the hole left by the disc.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 9, “Thermal Discharge Indicator (Red Disc)”, p. 9-9
notes.evidence: The thermal discharge indicator is connected to the fire container relief fitting and ejects a red disc to show when container contents have dumped overboard due to excessive heat. The agent discharges through the opening created when the disc blows out.
notes.example: Like a pressure cooker’s safety plug that pops and stays out, showing it has vented.

notes.front: What does the yellow disc discharge indicator show?
notes.back: That the flight crew activated the fire extinguishing system.
notes.explanation: The container then needs to be replaced before the next flight.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 9, “Yellow Disc Discharge Indicator”, p. 9-9
notes.evidence: If the flight crew activates the fire extinguisher system, a yellow disc is ejected from the skin of the aircraft fuselage. This is an indication for the maintenance crew that the fire extinguishing system was activated by the flight crew, and that the fire extinguishing container needs to be replaced before the next flight.
notes.example: Like the torn seal on a first-aid kit, telling the next user it has been opened.

notes.front: What happens when an engine fire switch is activated?
notes.back: The fuel control shuts off and the engine stops, the engine is isolated from aircraft systems, and extinguishing is activated.
notes.explanation: Some switches are pulled and turned; others are guarded push switches.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 9, “Fire Switch”, p. 9-9
notes.evidence: When the fire switch is activated, the following happens: the engine stops because the fuel control shuts off, the engine is isolated from the aircraft systems, and the fire extinguishing system is activated. Some aircraft use fire switches that need to be pulled and turned to activate the system, while others use a push-type switch with a guard.
notes.example: Like an emergency stop button on a machine, but also cutting the engine off from the aircraft and arming the fire bottles.

notes.front: What do engine fire warning systems give the flight crew when a fire is detected?
notes.back: A horn sounds and one or several warning lights illuminate.
notes.explanation: These indications stop when the fire is extinguished.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 9, “Warning Systems”, p. 9-10
notes.evidence: Visible and audible warning systems are installed in the flight deck to alert the flight crew. A horn sounds and one or several warning lights illuminate to alert the flight crew that an engine fire has been detected. These indications stop when the fire is extinguished.
notes.example: Like a building fire alarm with sounders and beacons, but in the flight deck.

notes.front: In the Powerplant handbook, what is a “fire zone”?
notes.back: An area the manufacturer designates as needing fire detection and/or extinguishing equipment and high inherent fire resistance.
notes.explanation: Potential fire zones of all multiengine aircraft now produced are protected by a fixed system.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 9, “Introduction”, p. 9-1
notes.evidence: A “fire zone” is an area or region of an aircraft designated by the manufacturer to require fire detection and/or fire extinguishing equipment and a high degree of inherent fire resistance.

notes.front: What does “fixed” mean in a fixed fire protection system?
notes.back: Permanently installed, as opposed to portable equipment such as a hand-held extinguisher.
notes.explanation: The handbook contrasts it with any type of portable fire extinguishing equipment.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 9, “Introduction”, p. 9-1
notes.evidence: The term “fixed” describes a permanently installed system in contrast to any type of portable fire extinguishing equipment, such as a hand-held fire extinguisher.

notes.front: Under the certification rules (parts 23 and 25), as the handbook summarises them, which aircraft must have an engine fire protection system?
notes.back: B) A twin with turbocharged reciprocating engines
notes.explanation: The list covers multiengine turbine aircraft, turbocharged multiengine piston aircraft, engines not readily visible from the flight deck, commuter and transport aircraft, and APU compartments.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 9, “Introduction”, p. 9-1
notes.evidence: engine fire protection systems are mandatory on: multiengine turbine-powered aircraft, multiengine reciprocating engine-powered aircraft incorporating turbochargers, aircraft with engine(s) located where they are not readily visible from the flight deck, all commuter and transport category aircraft, and the auxiliary power unit (APU) compartment of any aircraft incorporating an APU.
notes.choices:
A) A single-engine, normally aspirated trainer
B) A twin with turbocharged reciprocating engines
C) A normally aspirated piston twin with engines in view of the flight deck
D) A normally aspirated piston single used for glider towing
notes.choicesExplained: A: the handbook says many single and twin piston general aviation aircraft do not need one. C: only turbocharged piston twins are on the list, unless the engines are not readily visible. D: a normally aspirated single is not on the list; towing gliders does not change that.

notes.front: What two systems make up a complete fire protection system?
notes.back: A fire detection system and a fire extinguishing system.
notes.explanation: Detectors are placed in the zones to be monitored.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 9, “Components”, p. 9-1
notes.evidence: A complete fire protection system includes both a fire detection and a fire extinguishing system. To detect fires or overheat conditions, detectors are placed in the various zones to be monitored.

notes.front: What are the three kinds of detector the handbook says are used to detect aircraft fires?
notes.back: Overheat detectors, rate-of-temperature-rise detectors and flame detectors.
notes.explanation: Aircraft use one or more of these; other types, such as smoke detectors, are not used for engine fires.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 9, “Components”, p. 9-1
notes.evidence: Fires are detected in aircraft by using one or more of the following: overheat detectors, rate-oftemperature-rise detectors, and flame detectors.

notes.front: A student proposes smoke detectors for an engine nacelle. What does the handbook say smoke detectors are better suited to?
notes.back: D) Areas such as baggage compartments or lavatories, where materials burn slowly or smoulder
notes.explanation: Smoke and carbon monoxide detectors are used in fire protection, but not to detect engine fires.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 9, “Components”, p. 9-1
notes.evidence: For example, smoke detectors are better suited to monitor areas such as baggage compartments or lavatories, where materials burn slowly or smolder. Other types of detectors in this category include carbon monoxide detectors.
notes.choices:
A) Engine nacelles, as the primary engine fire detector
B) Replacing continuous loops on transport aircraft
C) Turbine tailpipes only
D) Areas such as baggage compartments or lavatories, where materials burn slowly or smoulder
notes.choicesExplained: A: the handbook says such detectors are not used for engine fires. B: transports almost exclusively use continuous thermal elements. C: the handbook does not place smoke detectors there.

notes.front: Do current-production aircraft rely on crew observation as a primary way to detect fire?
notes.back: No.
notes.explanation: The handbook states that current fire protection systems do not rely on it.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 9, “Components”, p. 9-1
notes.evidence: Fire protection systems on current-production aircraft do not rely on observation by crewmembers as a primary method of fire detection.

notes.front: What are two features of an ideal fire detector system?
notes.back: Any two, such as no false warnings in any condition, and rapid indication and accurate location of a fire.
notes.explanation: The handbook lists twelve features, among them indicating that a fire is out or has reignited.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 9, “Components”, p. 9-1
notes.evidence: 1. A system that does not cause false warnings under any flight or ground condition. 2. Rapid indication of a fire and accurate location of the fire. 3. Accurate indication that a fire is out. 4. Indication that a fire has reignited.

notes.front: According to the handbook’s ideal features, how many detector systems should an aircraft have per engine?
notes.back: A separate detector system for each engine.
notes.explanation: Each system should also turn on a flight deck light showing where the fire is and have an audible alarm.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 9, “Engine Fire Detection Systems”, p. 9-2
notes.evidence: 11. Each detector system should turn on a flight deck light, indicating the location of the fire, and have an audible alarm system. 12. A separate detector system for each engine.

notes.front: Spot detector or continuous-loop system: which monitors a fire zone with individual sensors?
notes.back: Spot detectors; continuous-loop systems use several loop-type sensors for more complete coverage.
notes.explanation: Continuous-loop systems are typically installed on transport type aircraft.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 9, “Engine Fire Detection Systems”, p. 9-2
notes.evidence: Spot detector systems use individual sensors to monitor a fire zone. Examples of spot detector systems are the thermal switch system, the thermocouple system, the optical fire detection system, and the pneumatic-based thermal fire detection system. Continuous loop systems are typically installed on transport type aircraft and provide more complete fire detection coverage by using several loop-type sensors.

notes.front: A thermal switch fire circuit has four switches around a nacelle. One section overheats. What happens?
notes.back: D) That switch closes and completes the circuit to the warning light
notes.explanation: Because the switches are in parallel with each other and in series with the light, any one closing lights the warning.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 9, “Thermal Switch System”, p. 9-2
notes.evidence: If the temperature rises above a set value in any one section of the circuit, the thermal switch closes, completing the light circuit to indicate a fire or overheat condition.
notes.choices:
A) All four switches must close before the light comes on
B) The light goes out
C) Nothing, unless the temperature is rising fast
D) That switch closes and completes the circuit to the warning light
notes.choicesExplained: A: they are in parallel, so any one completes the circuit. B: closing a switch completes the light circuit. C: rate of rise is the thermocouple principle, not the thermal switch.

notes.front: Who usually decides how many thermal switches a thermal switch system has?
notes.back: The aircraft manufacturer; no set number is required.
notes.explanation: Some installations connect all detectors to one light; others give each light its own switch.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 9, “Thermal Switch System”, p. 9-2
notes.evidence: No set number of thermal switches is required; the exact number usually is determined by the aircraft manufacturer. On some installations, all the thermal detectors are connected to one light; others may have a separate thermal switch for each indicator light.

notes.front: What does energising the test relay in a thermal switch fire circuit check?
notes.back: All the wiring and the light bulb, by completing a series circuit.
notes.explanation: Some warning lights are also push-to-test lights, tested by pushing the bulb in.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 9, “Thermal Switch System”, p. 9-2
notes.evidence: This is an additional safety feature. Energizing the test relay completes a series circuit and checks all the wiring and the light bulb.

notes.front: An engine compartment slowly overheats over many minutes. Which detection system does the handbook say will not warn of this?
notes.back: D) A thermocouple fire detection system
notes.explanation: A thermocouple system depends on the rate of temperature rise and does not warn when an engine slowly overheats.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 9, “Thermocouple Systems”, p. 9-2
notes.evidence: A thermocouple depends on the rate of temperature rise and does not give a warning when an engine slowly overheats or a short circuit develops.
notes.choices:
A) A thermal switch system
B) A Kidde continuous-loop system
C) A pneumatic continuous-loop detector
D) A thermocouple fire detection system
notes.choicesExplained: A: it closes at a set temperature, however slowly it is reached. B: it gives an overheat indication at a set resistance. C: it responds to an overall average temperature threshold.

notes.front: Into which three circuits is a thermocouple fire warning system’s wiring divided?
notes.back: The detector circuit, the alarm circuit and the test circuit.
notes.explanation: The system consists of a relay box, warning lights and thermocouples.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 9, “Thermocouple Systems”, p. 9-2
notes.evidence: The system consists of a relay box, warning lights, and thermocouples. The wiring system of these units may be divided into the following circuits: (1) the detector circuit, (2) the alarm circuit, and (3) the test circuit.

notes.front: During a long ground run, nacelle temperature rises gradually from normal engine heat. Why does a thermocouple fire system give no warning?
notes.back: A) Both junctions heat at the same rate, so no voltage results
notes.explanation: A fire heats the hot junction faster than the reference (cold) junction; a gradual rise heats both alike.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 9, “Thermocouple Systems”, p. 9-3
notes.evidence: In the engine compartment, there is a normal, gradual rise in temperature from engine operation; because it is gradual, both junctions heat at the same rate and no warning signal is given. If there is a fire, however, the hot junction heats more rapidly than the reference junction.
notes.choices:
A) Both junctions heat at the same rate, so no voltage results
B) The sensitive relay is locked out on the ground
C) The hot junction is shielded by its cage
D) Thermocouples only work above 900 °C
notes.choicesExplained: B: the handbook describes no such lockout. C: the cage leaves air free to reach the junction. D: the handbook sets no such threshold.

notes.front: In a thermocouple fire warning system, the sensitive relay closes whenever detector current is greater than {{c1::4 milliamperes (0.004 ampere)}}.
notes.back: 4 milliamperes (0.004 ampere).
notes.explanation: It then energises the slave relay, which lights the warning light.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 9, “Thermocouple Systems”, p. 9-3
notes.evidence: Any time the current is greater than 4 milliamperes (0.004 ampere), the sensitive relay closes. This completes a circuit from the aircraft power system to the coil of the slave relay. The slave relay then closes and completes the circuit to the warning light to give a visual fire warning.

notes.front: What limits the number of thermocouples in one fire detector circuit, and what is the usual resistance ceiling?
notes.back: Fire zone size and total circuit resistance, which usually does not exceed 5 ohms.
notes.explanation: The number depends on both the zone size and that resistance.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 9, “Thermocouple Systems”, p. 9-3
notes.evidence: The total number of thermocouples used in individual detector circuits depends on the size of the fire zones and the total circuit resistance, which usually does not exceed 5 ohms.

notes.front: Why is a resistor connected across the slave relay terminals in a thermocouple fire circuit?
notes.back: To absorb the coil’s self-induced voltage and prevent arcing across the sensitive relay points.
notes.explanation: The sensitive relay’s contacts are so fragile they burn or weld if arcing is permitted.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 9, “Thermocouple Systems”, p. 9-3
notes.evidence: The resistor connected across the slave relay terminals absorbs the coil’s self-induced voltage to prevent arcing across the points of the sensitive relay. The contacts of the sensitive relay are so fragile that they burn or weld if arcing is permitted.

notes.front: Thermal switch or continuous-loop versus thermocouple fire detection: which kind has rate-of-heat-rise sensitivity?
notes.back: Only the thermocouple system; continuous loops, versions of the thermal switch, are overheat systems with none.
notes.explanation: Thermal switch and continuous-loop units complete circuits at a certain temperature.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 9, “Continuous-Loop Detector Systems”, p. 9-3
notes.evidence: Continuous-loop systems are versions of the thermal switch system. They are overheat systems, heat-sensitive units that complete electrical circuits at a certain temperature. There is no rate-of-heatrise sensitivity in a continuous-loop system.

notes.front: In an infrared flame detector, what waveband does the filter pass to the sensing device?
notes.back: A tight waveband centred around 4.3 micrometres.
notes.explanation: The radiation slightly heats the sensing device, generating small thermoelectric voltages.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 9, “Optical Fire Detection Systems”, p. 9-3
notes.evidence: The filter allows only radiation in a tight waveband centered around 4.3 micrometers in the IR to pass on to the radiation-sensitive surface of the sensing device. The radiation striking the sensing device minutely raises its temperature causing small thermoelectric voltages to be generated.

notes.front: A helicopter’s infrared flame detector bay is exposed to sunlight when a panel is open. What does the handbook say about false alarms from such sources?
notes.back: D) The processing electronics ignore false alarm sources such as sunlight and incandescent lights
notes.explanation: The electronics match the time signature of hydrocarbon flames and ignore false sources like incandescent lights and sunlight.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 9, “Optical Fire Detection Systems”, p. 9-3
notes.evidence: The processing electronics is tailored exactly to the time signature of all known hydrocarbon flame sources and ignores false alarm sources, such as incandescent lights and sunlight.
notes.choices:
A) Sunlight always triggers it, so it must be covered
B) Only ultraviolet detectors can reject sunlight
C) It must be switched off in daylight
D) The processing electronics ignore false alarm sources such as sunlight and incandescent lights
notes.choicesExplained: A: the electronics are tailored to ignore sunlight. B: the handbook says this infrared detector’s electronics reject it. C: the handbook gives no such limitation.

notes.front: A pneumatic fire detector’s helium tube develops a leak. What does the handbook say happens?
notes.back: D) The integrity pressure switch opens and triggers the fault alarm
notes.explanation: The integrity switch is held closed by the gas pressure; losing pressure opens it and triggers a fault alarm.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 9, “Pneumatic Thermal Fire Detection”, p. 9-3
notes.evidence: The pneumatic detector integrity pressure switch opens and triggers the fault alarm if the pneumatic detector losses pressure, as in the case of a leak.
notes.choices:
A) A fire alarm is given
B) Nothing until the next heat event
C) The system switches to rate-of-rise sensing
D) The integrity pressure switch opens and triggers the fault alarm
notes.choicesExplained: A: loss of pressure triggers a fault alarm, not a fire alarm. B: the integrity switch reacts to the loss of pressure itself. C: pneumatic detectors have no such mode.

notes.front: What two sensing functions does a pneumatic continuous-loop detector have?
notes.back: An overall average temperature threshold and a localised discrete temperature increase from flame or hot gases.
notes.explanation: Both temperatures are factory set and not field adjustable.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Airframe (FAA-H-8083-31B), ch. 17, “Pneumatic Continuous-Loop Systems”, p. 17-6
notes.evidence: The pneumatic detector has two sensing functions. It responds to an overall average temperature threshold and to a localized discrete temperature increase caused by impinging flame or hot gasses. Both the average and discrete temperature are factory set and are not field adjustable.

notes.front: How are pneumatic continuous-loop systems typically installed on transport aircraft, and why?
notes.back: In a dual-loop design, to increase reliability.
notes.explanation: They have the same function as the Kidde system but work on a different principle.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Airframe (FAA-H-8083-31B), ch. 17, “Pneumatic Continuous-Loop Systems”, p. 17-6
notes.evidence: These systems are used for engine fire detection of transport type aircraft and have the same function as the Kidde system; however, they work on a different principle. They are typically used in a dual-loop design to increase reliability of the system.

notes.front: Why do large commercial aircraft almost exclusively use continuous thermal sensing elements for powerplant protection?
notes.back: Superior detection performance and coverage, and proven ruggedness in modern turbofan engines.
notes.explanation: The handbook gives these reasons for their near-exclusive use.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 9, “Continuous-Loop Detector Systems”, p. 9-3
notes.evidence: Large commercial aircraft almost exclusively use continuous thermal sensing elements for powerplant protection, since these systems offer superior detection performance and coverage, and they have the proven ruggedness to survive in the harsh environment of modern turbofan engines.

notes.front: In the Fenwal system, what happens when part of the element overheats?
notes.back: The eutectic salt’s resistance drops sharply and current flows between sheath and centre conductor.
notes.explanation: The control unit senses this current and actuates the output relay.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 9, “Fenwal Continuous-Loop System”, p. 9-4
notes.evidence: When an overheat condition occurs at any point along the element length, the resistance of the eutectic salt within the sensing element drops sharply, causing current to flow between the outer sheath and the center conductor. This current flow is sensed by the control unit, which produces a signal to actuate the output relay.

notes.front: A Fenwal system wired as a “loop” circuit develops one open circuit. What does the handbook say?
notes.back: D) It still signals fire or overheat
notes.explanation: In a loop circuit one open still signals; with multiple opens, only the section between breaks is lost.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 9, “Fenwal Continuous-Loop System”, p. 9-4
notes.evidence: The Fenwal system may be wired to employ a “loop” circuit. In this case, should an open circuit occur, the system still signals fire or overheat. If multiple open circuits occur, only that section between breaks becomes inoperative.
notes.choices:
A) The whole system becomes inoperative
B) It gives a false fire warning
C) Only the control unit fails
D) It still signals fire or overheat
notes.choicesExplained: A: with one open circuit the loop circuit still signals. B: the handbook says it still signals fire or overheat. C: the break is in the element wiring.

notes.front: In a Kidde continuous-loop system, how does the core’s resistance to ground change as it heats, and what does the control unit do?
notes.back: It decreases; at the overheat set point an overheat indication occurs, and further down, a fire warning.
notes.explanation: The fire detection control unit monitors this resistance.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 9, “Kidde Continuous-Loop System”, p. 9-4
notes.evidence: As the temperature of the core increases, electrical resistance to ground decreases. The fire detection control unit monitors this resistance. If the resistance decreases to the overheat set point, an overheat indication occurs in the flight deck.

notes.front: A Kidde loop’s resistance falls very quickly. How does the system tell a short from a fire?
notes.back: A) By the rate of change: resistance falls more quickly with an electrical short than with a fire
notes.explanation: The control unit monitors the loop’s resistance, and how fast it changes points to a short or a fire.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 9, “Kidde Continuous-Loop System”, p. 9-5
notes.evidence: The rate of change of resistance identifies an electrical short or a fire. The resistance decreases more quickly with an electrical short than with a fire.
notes.choices:
A) By the rate of change: resistance falls more quickly with an electrical short than with a fire
B) By the absolute temperature only
C) By a separate smoke sensor
D) It cannot tell them apart
notes.choicesExplained: B: the handbook names the rate of change of resistance. C: the Kidde loop does not use one. D: the rate of change identifies a short or a fire.

notes.front: Why can a thermistor sensing element be routed near non-hazardous hot spots without false alarms?
notes.back: It responds to a non-arithmetic average of resistance along its length, not a fixed alarm temperature.
notes.explanation: This lets the alarm point sit close to the maximum general ambient temperature.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 9, “Sensing Element”, p. 9-5
notes.evidence: As a result, the system responds not to a fixed alarm temperature but to the sum of the resistances (in parallel) that reflects a nonarithmetic “average.” The sensing element may be routed close to nonhazardous hot spots that may have a normal temperature well above the overall alarm temperature, without danger of causing a false alarm.

notes.front: What two levels of warning can a thermistor sensing element loop give?
notes.back: An overheat warning below the fire level, then a fire warning above anything leaking hot gas can reach.
notes.explanation: The overheat warning may come from leaking hot bleed air or combustion gas.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 9, “Combination Fire & Overheat Warning”, p. 9-5
notes.evidence: The first is an overheat warning at a temperature level below the fire warning, indicating a general engine compartment temperature rise, which could be caused by leakage of hot bleed air or combustion gas into the engine compartment.

notes.front: A technician presses the flight-deck fire test switch on a continuous-loop system and the alarm sounds. What has the test shown?
notes.back: C) Loop continuity, alarm indicator circuit integrity and proper functioning of the control circuits
notes.explanation: The test circuit simulates the resistance change of a fire; an alarm proves continuity, the alarm indicator circuit and the control circuits.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 9, “System Test”, p. 9-6
notes.evidence: that of the simulated fire and so the alarm is signaled. This demonstrates, in addition to the continuity of the sensing element loop, the integrity of the alarm indicator circuit and the proper functioning of the control circuits.
notes.choices:
A) Only that the warning bulb works
B) That the fire bottles are fully charged
C) Loop continuity, alarm indicator circuit integrity and proper functioning of the control circuits
D) That the thermistor has been recalibrated
notes.choicesExplained: A: the test also proves loop continuity and control circuits. B: container pressure is checked separately. D: thermistor properties do not change over the element’s life.

notes.front: At the preflight integrity test, one loop of a dual-loop engine fire detection system is found inoperative. What does the handbook allow?
notes.back: A) Disconnect that loop with the selector switch and dispatch on the other loop, deferring maintenance
notes.explanation: Since the single operative loop meets all fire detector requirements, the aircraft can be dispatched safely with maintenance deferred.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 9, “Dual-Loop Systems”, p. 9-6
notes.evidence: Should one of the two loops be found inoperative at the preflight integrity test, a flight deck selector switch disconnects that loop and allows the signal from the other loop alone to activate the fire warning. Since the single operative loop meets all fire detector requirements, the aircraft can be safely dispatched, and maintenance deferred to a more convenient time.
notes.choices:
A) Disconnect that loop with the selector switch and dispatch on the other loop, deferring maintenance
B) Leave both loops selected with “AND” logic
C) The aircraft must not fly until both loops work
D) Rely on crew observation instead
notes.choicesExplained: B: the dead loop would then block any fire warning. C: one operative loop meets all detector requirements. D: current systems do not use observation as a primary method.

notes.front: In a dual-loop system with automatic self-interrogation, one loop signals “fire” and the other loop tests operative. What happens?
notes.back: D) The fire signal is suppressed, because the operative loop would have signalled a real fire
notes.explanation: Self-interrogation tests the other loop; if it works, the single “fire” signal is suppressed, and if it has failed, a fire signal is given.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 9, “Automatic Self-Interrogation”, p. 9-6
notes.evidence: Should the control circuit from a single loop signal “fire,” the self-interrogation circuit automatically tests the functioning of the other loop. If it tests operative, the circuit suppresses the fire signal (because the operative loop would have signaled if a fire existed). If, however, the other loop tests inoperative, the circuit outputs a fire signal.
notes.choices:
A) A fire warning is given at once
B) Both loops are disconnected
C) The crew must switch loops by hand
D) The fire signal is suppressed, because the operative loop would have signalled a real fire
notes.choicesExplained: A: that happens only if the other loop tests inoperative. B: the circuit tests, then decides; it does not disconnect both. C: self-interrogation does the switching automatically.

notes.front: In the handbook’s transport example, what happens if both engine fire detection loops fail?
notes.back: Advisory and status messages show, and the fire detection system does not operate.
notes.explanation: If only one loop fails, the fire detection card, which monitors both loops, changes to single-loop operation if necessary.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 9, “Single/Dual Loop Operation”, p. 9-14
notes.evidence: The card changes to single-loop operation, if necessary. If both detection loops fail, an advisory message and status messages are displayed, and the fire detection system does not operate.

notes.front: What are two of the designated fire zones of a powerplant installation?
notes.back: Any two, such as the engine power section, the engine accessory section and any APU compartment.
notes.explanation: The handbook lists seven, including fuel-burning heater installations and parts of turbine engines.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 9, “Fire Zones”, p. 9-7
notes.evidence: The powerplant installation has several designated fire zones: (1) the engine power section; (2) the engine accessory section; (3) except for reciprocating engines, any complete powerplant compartment in which no isolation is provided between the engine power section and the engine accessory section; (4) any APU compartment;

notes.front: Which turbine engine area does the handbook list as a designated fire zone only when it contains lines or components carrying flammable fluids or gases?
notes.back: D) The combustor, turbine and tailpipe sections
notes.explanation: Combustor, turbine and tailpipe sections are fire zones when they contain lines or components carrying flammable fluids or gases.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 9, “Fire Zones”, p. 9-7
notes.evidence: (5) any fuel-burning heater and other combustion equipment installation; (6) the compressor and accessory sections of turbine engines; and (7) combustor, turbine, and tailpipe sections of turbine engine installations that contain lines or components carrying flammable fluids or gases.
notes.choices:
A) The engine accessory section
B) The compressor and accessory sections
C) Any APU compartment
D) The combustor, turbine and tailpipe sections
notes.choicesExplained: A: it is a designated fire zone in its own right. B: these are listed as fire zones without that condition. C: every APU compartment is a designated fire zone.

notes.front: On what basis does the Airframe handbook classify powerplant compartments into zone classes?
notes.back: The airflow through them.
notes.explanation: The classes run from heavy airflow to little or none, plus a class for unusual construction.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Airframe (FAA-H-8083-31B), ch. 17, “Fire Zones”, p. 17-7
notes.evidence: Fire Zones Powerplant compartments are classified into zones based on the airflow through them.

notes.front: What is a Class A fire zone?
notes.back: An area of heavy airflow past regular arrangements of similarly shaped obstructions.
notes.explanation: The power section of a reciprocating engine is usually this type.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Airframe (FAA-H-8083-31B), ch. 17, “Fire Zones”, p. 17-7
notes.evidence: Class A zone—area of heavy airflow past regular arrangements of similarly shaped obstructions. The power section of a reciprocating engine is usually of this type.

notes.front: What is a Class B fire zone?
notes.back: An area of heavy airflow past aerodynamically clean obstructions.
notes.explanation: Examples include heat exchanger ducts and exhaust manifold shrouds.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Airframe (FAA-H-8083-31B), ch. 17, “Fire Zones”, p. 17-7
notes.evidence: 2. Class B zone—area of heavy airflow past aerodynamically clean obstructions. Included in this type are heat exchanger ducts, exhaust manifold shrouds,

notes.front: What is a Class C fire zone?
notes.back: An area of relatively low airflow.
notes.explanation: An engine accessory compartment separated from the power section is an example.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Airframe (FAA-H-8083-31B), ch. 17, “Fire Zones”, p. 17-7
notes.evidence: 3. Class C zone—area of relatively low airflow. An engine accessory compartment separated from the power section is an example of this type of zone.

notes.front: What is a Class D fire zone?
notes.back: An area of very little or no airflow.
notes.explanation: Wing compartments and wheel wells with little ventilation are examples.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Airframe (FAA-H-8083-31B), ch. 17, “Fire Zones”, p. 17-7
notes.evidence: 4. Class D zone—area of very little or no airflow. These include wing compartments and wheel wells where little ventilation is provided.

notes.front: What is a Class X fire zone, and how much agent do tests show it needs?
notes.back: Heavy airflow with unusual construction; about double the agent needed for Class A zones.
notes.explanation: Deep recesses and pockets make uniform distribution of the agent very difficult.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Airframe (FAA-H-8083-31B), ch. 17, “Fire Zones”, p. 17-7
notes.evidence: Class X zone—area of heavy airflow and of unusual construction, making uniform distribution of the extinguishing agent very difficult. Areas containing deeply recessed spaces and pockets between large structural formers are of this type. Tests indicate agent requirements to be double those for Class A zones.

notes.front: An engine accessory compartment is separated from the power section and has relatively low airflow. Which fire zone class is it?
notes.back: A) Class C
notes.explanation: A separated accessory compartment of relatively low airflow is the handbook’s example of a Class C zone.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Airframe (FAA-H-8083-31B), ch. 17, “Fire Zones”, p. 17-7
notes.evidence: 3. Class C zone—area of relatively low airflow. An engine accessory compartment separated from the power section is an example of this type of zone.
notes.choices:
A) Class C
B) Class A
C) Class D
D) Class X
notes.choicesExplained: B: Class A is heavy airflow past similar obstructions, like a piston power section. C: Class D has very little or no airflow, like wheel wells. D: Class X is heavy airflow with unusual construction.

notes.front: A transport aircraft designer asks whether an APU fire zone may have a one-shot extinguishing system. What does the handbook say?
notes.back: D) Yes: an individual one-shot system may be used for APUs, fuel-burning heaters and other combustion equipment
notes.explanation: APUs, fuel-burning heaters and other combustion equipment may use a one-shot system; each “other” designated fire zone needs two discharges.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 9, “Engine Fire Extinguishing System”, p. 9-7
notes.evidence: An individual one-shot system may be used for APUs, fuel burning heaters, and other combustion equipment. For each “other” designated fire zone, two discharges (two-shot system) must be provided, each of which produces adequate agent concentration.
notes.choices:
A) No: every zone on a transport needs two discharges
B) No: APUs need a portable extinguisher only
C) Yes, but only on commuter aircraft
D) Yes: an individual one-shot system may be used for APUs, fuel-burning heaters and other combustion equipment
notes.choicesExplained: A: APUs, heaters and combustion equipment are the stated exception. B: the handbook allows a fixed one-shot system. C: the one-shot allowance is not limited to commuters.

notes.front: How are fixed engine fire extinguisher systems designed to put out a fire?
notes.back: By diluting the atmosphere with an inert agent that does not support combustion.
notes.explanation: This applies to the fixed systems used in most engine fire protection systems.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 9, “Fire Extinguishing Agents”, p. 9-7
notes.evidence: The fixed fire extinguisher systems used in most engine fire protection systems are designed to dilute the atmosphere with an inert agent that does not support combustion.

notes.front: What does discharged Halon 1301 do to the materials it contacts?
notes.back: Nothing: it is non-corrosive, does not affect materials and needs no clean-up.
notes.explanation: It is the current extinguishing agent for commercial aircraft, though a replacement is under development.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 9, “Fire Extinguishing Agents”, p. 9-7
notes.evidence: Noncorrosive, Halon 1301 does not affect the material it contacts and requires no clean-up when discharged. Halon 1301 is the current extinguishing agent for commercial aircraft, but a replacement is under development.

notes.front: Why is only recycled Halon 1301 currently available?
notes.back: Because Halon 1301 depletes the ozone layer.
notes.explanation: It stays in use until a suitable replacement is developed.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 9, “Fire Extinguishing Agents”, p. 9-7
notes.evidence: Because Halon 1301 depletes the ozone layer only recycled Halon 1301 is currently available. Halon 1301 is used until a suitable replacement is developed.

notes.front: Which Halon is the total flooding agent suited to a fixed engine fire system, and which is the streaming agent?
notes.back: D) Halon 1301 is the total flooding agent; Halon 1211 is the streaming agent
notes.explanation: The Airframe handbook names Halon 1301 a total flooding agent and Halon 1211 a streaming agent.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Airframe (FAA-H-8083-31B), ch. 17, “Halogenated Hydrocarbons”, p. 17-9
notes.evidence: Two types of Halons are employed in aviation: Halon 1301(CBrF 3) a total flooding agent, and Halon 1211 (CBrClF2) a streaming agent.
notes.choices:
A) Halon 1211 floods; Halon 1301 streams
B) Both are streaming agents
C) Both are total flooding agents
D) Halon 1301 is the total flooding agent; Halon 1211 is the streaming agent
notes.choicesExplained: A: the roles are the other way round. B: Halon 1301 is a total flooding agent. C: Halon 1211 is a streaming agent.

notes.front: A fire involves burning metal (a Class D fire). May a Halon extinguisher be used?
notes.back: D) No: Halon agents may react vigorously with the burning metal
notes.explanation: Halons control Class A, B or C fires, but the handbook says not to use them on Class D fires.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Airframe (FAA-H-8083-31B), ch. 17, “Halogenated Hydrocarbons”, p. 17-9
notes.evidence: Class A, B, or C fires are appropriately controlled with Halons. However, do not use Halons on a class D fire. Halon agents may react vigorously with the burning metal.
notes.choices:
A) Only after cooling with carbon dioxide
B) Yes: Halons suit all fire classes
C) Yes, if it is Halon 1301
D) No: Halon agents may react vigorously with the burning metal
notes.choicesExplained: A: carbon dioxide cannot put out magnesium or titanium fires either. B: Halons suit Class A, B or C only. C: the warning covers Halons generally.

notes.front: A ramp crew is choosing the kind of extinguisher to keep by the aircraft for fires on its exterior, such as an engine or APU fire. Which agent does the handbook say ramp extinguishers most often use?
notes.back: B) Carbon dioxide
notes.explanation: Carbon dioxide is most often used in ramp extinguishers for exterior engine or APU fires, and has long been used on flammable fluid and electrical fires.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 9, “Fire Extinguishing Agents”, p. 9-7
notes.evidence: It is most often used in fire extinguishers that are available on the ramp to fight fires on the exterior of the aircraft, such as engine or APU fires. CO2 has been used for many years to extinguish flammable fluid fires and fires involving electrical equipment.
notes.choices:
A) Water
B) Carbon dioxide
C) Dry powder
D) Specialised dry powder for Class D
notes.choicesExplained: A: water best suits Class A fires by cooling and soaking. C: the handbook does not name it for ramp engine fires. D: that is for burning metals.

notes.front: What hazard does carbon dioxide pose to people at fire extinguishing concentrations?
notes.back: Unconsciousness and death by suffocation if breathed for 20 to 30 minutes.
notes.explanation: The handbook calls it only mildly toxic otherwise.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Airframe (FAA-H-8083-31B), ch. 17, “Inert Cold Gases”, p. 17-10
notes.evidence: CO2 is considered only mildly toxic, but it can cause unconsciousness and death by suffocation if the victim is allowed to breathe CO2 in fire extinguishing concentrations for 20 to 30 minutes.

notes.front: Which fires does the handbook say carbon dioxide cannot put out?
notes.back: Fires of chemicals with their own oxygen supply, such as cellulose nitrate, and magnesium and titanium fires.
notes.explanation: Cellulose nitrate is used in some aircraft paints.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Airframe (FAA-H-8083-31B), ch. 17, “Inert Cold Gases”, p. 17-10
notes.evidence: CO2 is not effective as an extinguishing agent on fires involving chemicals containing their own oxygen supply, such as cellulose nitrate (used in some aircraft paints). Also, fires involving magnesium and titanium cannot be extinguished by CO2.

notes.front: During a false start, a fire develops inside a turbine engine’s tailpipe. What does the handbook say to try first?
notes.back: C) Motor the engine with the starter to blow the fire out
notes.explanation: Internal tailpipe fires during shutdown or false starts can be blown out by motoring with the starter; agent is used if the fire persists.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 9, “Turbine Engine Ground Fire Protection”, p. 9-8
notes.evidence: Internal engine tailpipe fires that take place during engine shutdown or false starts can be blown out by motoring the engine with the starter. A running engine can be accelerated to rated speed to achieve the same result. If such a fire persists, a fire extinguishing agent can be directed into the tailpipe.
notes.choices:
A) Discharge the fixed engine fire bottles at once
B) Flood the tailpipe with carbon dioxide until cold
C) Motor the engine with the starter to blow the fire out
D) Open the cowls and wait
notes.choicesExplained: A: agent is directed into the tailpipe only if the fire persists. B: excessive carbon dioxide can shrink the housing on the turbine. D: the handbook says the fire can be blown out by motoring.

notes.front: Why should excessive carbon dioxide not be used on a turbine engine fire?
notes.back: Its cooling effect can shrink the turbine housing onto the turbine and cause the engine to disintegrate.
notes.explanation: The same caution applies to other agents that have a cooling effect.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 9, “Turbine Engine Ground Fire Protection”, p. 9-8
notes.evidence: It should be remembered that excessive use of CO2, or other agents that have a cooling effect, can shrink the turbine housing on the turbine and cause the engine to disintegrate.

notes.front: Why are most aircraft fire extinguisher containers spherical?
notes.back: A sphere provides the lightest weight possible.
notes.explanation: Cylindrical containers are available where space is limited.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 9, “Containers”, p. 9-8
notes.evidence: Most aircraft containers are spherical in design, which provides the lightest weight possible. However, cylindrical shapes are available where space limitations are a factor.

notes.front: A fire bottle is exposed to excessive heat in a nacelle. What protects it from exceeding its test pressure?
notes.back: D) Its temperature/pressure-sensitive safety relief diaphragm
notes.explanation: Each container has a safety relief diaphragm that stops its pressure exceeding test pressure if exposed to excessive temperatures.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 9, “Containers”, p. 9-8
notes.evidence: Each container incorporates a temperature/pressure sensitive safety relief diaphragm that prevents container pressure from exceeding container test pressure in the event of exposure to excessive temperatures.
notes.choices:
A) The squib, which fires automatically
B) The two-way check valve
C) The yellow disc
D) Its temperature/pressure-sensitive safety relief diaphragm
notes.choicesExplained: A: the squib fires only when the crew or system commands it. B: that stops agent backing into an emptied container. C: the yellow disc shows a crew-commanded discharge.

notes.front: Which Airman Certification Standards skill for engine fire protection involves hydrostatic testing?
notes.back: Inspecting a fire extinguisher container and determining its hydrostatic test requirements.
notes.explanation: It is listed next to the skills of inspecting flame detectors and checking fire warning press-to-test.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Mechanic General, Airframe, and Powerplant Airman Certification Standards (FAA-S-ACS-1), “III. Powerplant, E. Engine Fire Protection Systems”, p. 49
notes.evidence: AM.III.E.S11 Inspect fire extinguisher container and determine hydrostatic test requirements. AM.III.E.S12 Inspect flame detectors for operation. AM.III.E.S13 Check operation of fire warning press-to-test and troubleshoot faults.

notes.front: A discharge valve is for a hermetically sealed container. Which cartridge disc-release technique does the handbook say is used?
notes.back: A) A direct explosive impact cartridge that fragments a prestressed steel diaphragm
notes.explanation: Standard release uses an explosive-driven slug; high-temperature or hermetically sealed units use a direct explosive impact cartridge.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 9, “Discharge Valves”, p. 9-8
notes.evidence: Standard release type uses a slug driven by explosive energy to rupture a segmented closure disc. For high temperature or hermetically sealed units, a direct explosive impact type cartridge is used, which applies fragmentation impact to rupture a prestressed corrosionresistant steel diaphragm.
notes.choices:
A) A direct explosive impact cartridge that fragments a prestressed steel diaphragm
B) A standard release slug that ruptures a segmented disc
C) A solenoid-operated seat valve only
D) A thermal red disc
notes.choicesExplained: B: that is the standard type, not the one for sealed units. C: such assemblies exist but are not the sealed-unit cartridge. D: that is a discharge indicator, not a release technique.

notes.front: A container has a combination gauge switch. What does it provide?
notes.back: C) A visual reading of container pressure and an electrical signal if pressure is lost
notes.explanation: A combination gauge switch shows pressure and signals loss of pressure electrically, so no discharge indicators are needed.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 9, “Pressure Indication”, p. 9-8
notes.evidence: A combination gauge switch visually indicates actual container pressure and also provides an electrical signal if container pressure is lost, precluding the need for discharge indicators.
notes.choices:
A) Only a visual pressure reading
B) Only a thermal discharge indication
C) A visual reading of container pressure and an electrical signal if pressure is lost
D) Automatic discharge when pressure is low
notes.choicesExplained: A: it also signals electrically on loss of pressure. B: that is the red disc’s job. D: it indicates; it does not discharge.

notes.front: What simple visual gauge is typically used to show fire extinguisher container charge?
notes.back: A vibration-resistant helical Bourdon-type indicator.
notes.explanation: A diaphragm-type low-pressure switch is common on hermetically sealed containers.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 9, “Pressure Indication”, p. 9-8
notes.evidence: A simple visually indicated gauge is available, typically a vibration-resistant helical bourdon-type indicator. [see Figure 9-9] A combination gauge switch visually indicates actual container pressure

notes.front: You read a fire extinguisher container’s pressure and the ambient temperature, and plot them on its pressure-temperature chart. The point falls outside the limits. What does the handbook say?
notes.back: B) Replace the extinguisher container
notes.explanation: Container pressure must fall within the chart’s minimum and maximum for the ambient temperature; otherwise the container is replaced.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 9, “Fire Extinguisher System Maintenance Practices”, p. 9-12
notes.evidence: Changes of pressure with ambient temperatures must also fall within prescribed limits. The graph shown in Figure 9-18 is typical of the pressure temperature curve graphs that provide maximum and minimum gauge readings. If the pressure does not fall within the graph limits, the extinguisher container is replaced.
notes.choices:
A) Top it up with nitrogen on the aircraft
B) Replace the extinguisher container
C) Accept it if the temperature is below freezing
D) Replace only the squib
notes.choicesExplained: A: the handbook says to replace a container outside the limits. C: pressure must be within limits at the ambient temperature. D: the squib does not affect container pressure.

image.alt: Line chart of fire extinguisher container pressure in psig (0 to 900) against temperature in °F (−40 to 80). Two rising curves: the upper, maximum gauge reading, runs from about 400 psig at −40 °F to about 730 psig at 80 °F; the lower, minimum gauge reading, runs from about 250 psig at −40 °F to about 580 psig at 80 °F. An acceptable reading lies between the two curves at the ambient temperature.
image.credit: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), Figure 9-18

notes.front: In the handbook’s transport example, a fire container has two squibs in its discharge assembly. Why two?
notes.back: A) One for each engine, so the bottle can discharge to either engine
notes.explanation: The handbook gives one squib for each engine, so one bottle can be fired into either engine by turning the fire switch to either discharge position.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 9, “Squib”, p. 9-16
notes.evidence: A fire container has two squibs, one for each engine. The squib is an electrically operated explosive device. When the squib is activated, it fires a slug through the breakable disc, and nitrogen pressure inside the bottle pushes the Halon through the discharge port.
notes.choices:
A) One for each engine, so the bottle can discharge to either engine
B) One opens the bottle and one closes it
C) One for flight, one for ground testing
D) One is a spare in case the first fails to fire
notes.choicesExplained: B: a squib only opens the discharge path. C: the handbook does not describe this. D: the handbook gives one per engine.

notes.front: During an inspection you need the unexpired service life of a discharge cartridge. What does the handbook say?
notes.back: C) It is calculated from the manufacturer’s date stamp, usually on the cartridge face
notes.explanation: Cartridge service life, usually in years (5 years or more is available), runs from the date stamp; the cartridge usually must be removed to see it.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Airframe (FAA-H-8083-31B), ch. 17, “Discharge Cartridges”, p. 17-19
notes.evidence: The service life of fire extinguisher discharge cartridges is determined from the manufacturer’s date stamp, which is usually placed on the face of the cartridge. The cartridge service life recommended by the manufacturer is usually in terms of years. Cartridges are available with a service life of 5 years or more.
notes.choices:
A) Cartridges have unlimited life until fired
B) It is set by flight hours logged on the bottle
C) It is calculated from the manufacturer’s date stamp, usually on the cartridge face
D) It is read from the container pressure gauge
notes.choicesExplained: A: the manufacturer recommends a service life. B: service life is usually given in years from the date stamp. D: the gauge shows agent charge, not cartridge life.

notes.front: A discharge cartridge was removed from one discharge valve. A technician wants to fit it in a different valve. What does the handbook say?
notes.back: A) Do not: the contact point protrusion varies, so continuity might not exist
notes.explanation: A used plug indented by a long contact point may not make contact in a valve with a shorter one, so a removed cartridge stays with its own valve.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Airframe (FAA-H-8083-31B), ch. 17, “Agent Containers”, p. 17-20
notes.evidence: If a cartridge is removed from a discharge valve for any reason, it should not be used in another discharge valve assembly, since the distance the contact point protrudes may vary with each unit.
notes.choices:
A) Do not: the contact point protrusion varies, so continuity might not exist
B) Fit it if it is within its service life
C) Fit it after cleaning the contacts
D) Fit it only in a valve of the same part number
notes.choicesExplained: B: service life is not the issue; contact protrusion is. C: cleaning does not fix a mismatched contact length. D: the handbook says not to use it in another valve assembly at all.

notes.front: Which squib-related risk does the Airman Certification Standards name for engine fire protection?
notes.back: Maintenance on circuits associated with electrically activated container discharge cartridges (squibs).
notes.explanation: The standards also name container discharge cartridges and extinguishing agents as risks.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Mechanic General, Airframe, and Powerplant Airman Certification Standards (FAA-S-ACS-1), “III. Powerplant, E. Engine Fire Protection Systems”, p. 49
notes.evidence: AM.III.E.R1 Container discharge cartridges. AM.III.E.R2 Extinguishing agents. AM.III.E.R3 Maintenance on circuits associated with electrically-activated container discharge cartridges (squibs).

notes.front: What do discharge indicators provide on a fire extinguishing system?
notes.back: Immediate visual evidence that a container has discharged.
notes.explanation: Two kinds are available, thermal and discharge, both for aircraft skin mounting.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 9, “Discharge Indicators”, p. 9-9
notes.evidence: Discharge indicators provide immediate visual evidence of container discharge on fire extinguishing systems. Two kinds of indicators can be furnished: thermal and discharge. Both types are designed for aircraft and skin mounting.

notes.front: On a walk-round, you find the red disc missing from the fuselage skin, and the crew report no fire bottle use. What does this tell you?
notes.back: A) The container dumped overboard from excessive heat and must be replaced before the next flight
notes.explanation: The red disc blows out when excessive heat dumps the contents overboard through the relief fitting; the container must be replaced before the next flight.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 9, “Thermal Discharge Indicator (Red Disc)”, p. 9-9
notes.evidence: The agent discharges through the opening created when the disc blows out. This gives the flight and maintenance crews an indication that the fire extinguisher container needs to be replaced before the next flight.
notes.choices:
A) The container dumped overboard from excessive heat and must be replaced before the next flight
B) Nothing: the red disc is decorative
C) The crew fired the bottle and forgot
D) The squib needs replacing, not the container
notes.choicesExplained: B: it is a thermal discharge indicator. C: crew discharge ejects the yellow disc. D: the handbook says the container needs replacing.

notes.front: On a walk-round, the yellow disc is missing from the fuselage skin. What does this indicate?
notes.back: C) The flight crew activated the fire extinguishing system; the container must be replaced before the next flight
notes.explanation: The yellow disc is ejected when the crew fires the system, telling maintenance to replace the container.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 9, “Yellow Disc Discharge Indicator”, p. 9-9
notes.evidence: If the flight crew activates the fire extinguisher system, a yellow disc is ejected from the skin of the aircraft fuselage. This is an indication for the maintenance crew that the fire extinguishing system was activated by the flight crew
notes.choices:
A) The container overheated and vented
B) A detector loop has failed
C) The flight crew activated the fire extinguishing system; the container must be replaced before the next flight
D) The container is due a hydrostatic test
notes.choicesExplained: A: heat venting ejects the red disc. B: loop faults show in the flight deck, not by a skin disc. D: the disc shows discharge, not a test date.

notes.front: Red disc or yellow disc: which shows a discharge the flight crew commanded, and which a heat discharge?
notes.back: Yellow: crew activation. Red: contents dumped overboard from excessive heat.
notes.explanation: Either way, the container needs to be replaced before the next flight.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 9, “Discharge Indicators”, p. 9-9
notes.evidence: ejects a red disc to show when container contents have dumped overboard due to excessive heat.

notes.front: An engine is on fire but the fire switch will not pull: the detection system has failed and its solenoid is not energised. What does the handbook describe?
notes.back: C) Push the fire override switch so the fire switch can be pulled
notes.explanation: A lock releases the fire switch only when a fire is detected; the override switch lets the crew release it manually.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 9, “Engine Fire Switches”, p. 9-16
notes.evidence: When the fire detection system malfunctions or the solenoid is defective, and the flight crew wants to extinguish an engine fire, someone must push the fire override switch. The fire override switch allows the fire switch to be pulled when the solenoid is not energized.
notes.choices:
A) Wait for the lock to time out
B) Break the switch guard and force it
C) Push the fire override switch so the fire switch can be pulled
D) Use the portable flight-deck extinguisher on the engine
notes.choicesExplained: A: the lock releases on a detected fire or by override. B: the override exists for this case. D: the fixed system reaches the nacelle.

notes.front: In the handbook’s transport example, what are two things a pulled engine fire switch does to isolate the engine?
notes.back: Any two, such as closing the fuel spar valve, closing the hydraulic pump shutoff valve and tripping the generator field.
notes.explanation: The handbook lists eight such actions.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 9, “Engine Fire Switches”, p. 9-16
notes.evidence: Closes the fuel spar valve. • Deenergizes the engine fuel metering unit (FMU) cutoff solenoid. • Closes the engine hydraulic pump shutoff valve. • Depressurizes the engine driven hydraulic pump valve. • Closes the pressure regulator and shutoff valve. • Removes power from thrust reverser isolation valve. • Trips the generator field.

notes.front: In the handbook’s transport example, the crew pulls the fire switch but the fire warning stays on. What next?
notes.back: D) Turn the switch to a discharge position and hold it against the stop for one second
notes.explanation: Holding the switch at a discharge position for one second fires the squib; if the first bottle fails, the other discharge position fires the second.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 9, “Engine Fire Operation”, p. 9-17
notes.evidence: If the fire warnings do not go away when the switch is pulled, position the switch to the DISCH 1 or DISCH 2 position, and hold the switch against the stop for one second. This fires the squib in the fire extinguisher container and releases the fire extinguishing agent into the engine nacelle.
notes.choices:
A) Push the switch back in and restart the engine
B) Press the fire override switch
C) Wait for the warning to clear by itself
D) Turn the switch to a discharge position and hold it against the stop for one second
notes.choicesExplained: A: the handbook gives no restart step. B: the override only releases a locked switch. C: the handbook says to discharge a bottle.

notes.front: An APU is running on the ground with no engines running and nobody in the flight deck when it catches fire. What does the handbook’s transport example do?
notes.back: B) The APU fire extinguisher discharges automatically
notes.explanation: In unattended mode the APU extinguisher discharges automatically; in attended mode the crew discharges it manually.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 9, “APU Fire Detection & Extinguishing System”, p. 9-18
notes.evidence: If there is an APU fire in the unattended mode, the fire extinguisher discharges automatically. The APU operates in the attended mode when at least one engine is running. If there is an APU fire in this mode, the crew discharges the bottle manually.
notes.choices:
A) Nothing until a crew member pulls the fire switch
B) The APU fire extinguisher discharges automatically
C) It sounds an alarm but cannot discharge
D) It discharges an engine bottle into the APU
notes.choicesExplained: A: manual discharge is for attended mode, with an engine running. C: in unattended mode the bottle discharges automatically. D: the APU has its own bottle.

notes.front: Why are fire detector sensing elements at high risk of damage during maintenance?
