notes.back: They are small and located in many high-activity areas around the engine.
notes.explanation: The handbook says location and small size together increase the chance of damage.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 9, “Fire Detection System Maintenance”, p. 9-10
notes.evidence: Fire detector sensing elements are located in many highactivity areas around aircraft engines. Their location, together with their small size, increases the chance of damage to the sensing elements during maintenance.

notes.front: What are two defects to look for when inspecting continuous-loop sensing elements?
notes.back: Any two, such as crushed or broken sections, abrasion from rubbing, and stray safety wire that could short terminals.
notes.explanation: The handbook’s list also includes grommet condition, dents and kinks, and loose end nuts.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 9, “Fire Detection System Maintenance”, p. 9-10
notes.evidence: 1. Cracked or broken sections caused by crushing or squeezing between inspection plates, cowl panels, or engine components. 2. Abrasion caused by rubbing of the element on cowling, accessories, or structural members. 3. Pieces of safety wire or other metal particles that may short the spot-detector terminals.

notes.front: A sensing element has a dent within the manufacturer’s acceptable limits. A colleague wants to straighten it. What does the handbook say?
notes.back: D) Do not straighten it: stresses could be set up that cause tubing failure
notes.explanation: Acceptable dents and kinks are left alone, since straightening may set up stresses that cause tubing failure.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 9, “Fire Detection System Maintenance”, p. 9-10
notes.evidence: No attempt should be made to straighten any acceptable dent or kink, since stresses may be set up that could cause tubing failure.
notes.choices:
A) Straighten it carefully by hand
B) Straighten it with a tubing roller
C) Replace the element at once
D) Do not straighten it: stresses could be set up that cause tubing failure
notes.choicesExplained: A: no attempt should be made to straighten an acceptable dent. B: any straightening can set up damaging stresses. C: the dent is within acceptable limits.

notes.front: You are re-routing a sensing element on a straight run. What clamp spacing does the handbook give as usual?
notes.back: B) About 8 to 10 inches, as specified by the manufacturer
notes.explanation: Long unsupported sections may vibrate enough to break; the first clamp is usually 4 to 6 inches from an end connector.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Airframe (FAA-H-8083-31B), ch. 17, “Fire Detection System Maintenance”, p. 17-18
notes.evidence: Long, unsupported sections may permit excessive vibration that can cause breakage. The distance between clamps on straight runs, usually about 8 to 10 inches, is specified by each manufacturer. At end connectors, the first support clamp usually is located about 4 to 6 inches from the end connector fittings.
notes.choices:
A) About 2 to 3 inches
B) About 8 to 10 inches, as specified by the manufacturer
C) About 18 to 24 inches
D) No clamps are needed on straight runs
notes.choicesExplained: A: the handbook gives 8 to 10 inches on straight runs. C: long unsupported sections may vibrate and break. D: routing and clamping must be inspected carefully.

notes.front: Near connectors, how much straight run is kept before a sensing element bend, and what bend radius is normal?
notes.back: A straight run of one inch, then an optimum bend radius of 3 inches.
notes.explanation: These are the usual figures; the manufacturer’s instructions govern.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Airframe (FAA-H-8083-31B), ch. 17, “Fire Detection System Maintenance”, p. 17-18
notes.evidence: In most cases, a straight run of one inch is maintained from all connectors before a bend is started, and an optimum bend radius of 3 inches is normally adhered to.

notes.front: How should grommets be installed on a sensing element?
notes.back: Both ends centred on the clamp, with the split end facing the outside of the nearest bend.
notes.explanation: Clamps and grommets should fit the element snugly.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 9, “Fire Detection System Maintenance”, p. 9-11
notes.evidence: 10. Grommets should be installed on the sensing element so that both ends are centered on its clamp. The split end of the grommet should face the outside of the nearest bend. Clamps and grommets should fit the element snugly.

notes.front: When must copper crush gaskets at sensing element connection joints be replaced?
notes.back: Any time a connection is separated.
notes.explanation: End nuts are also checked for tightness and safety wire, and loose nuts retorqued.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 9, “Fire Detection System Maintenance”, p. 9-10
notes.evidence: Loose nuts should be retorqued to the value specified by the manufacturer’s instructions. Some types of sensing element connection joints require the use of copper crush gaskets, which should be replaced any time a connection is separated.

notes.front: An engine fire warning comes and goes on the ground with no fire. What does the handbook give as the most common cause?
notes.back: D) An intermittent short in the detector system wiring
notes.explanation: Loose or frayed wires, or an element rubbed through its insulation, can cause such shorts.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 9, “Fire Detection System Troubleshooting”, p. 9-11
notes.evidence: Intermittent alarms are most often caused by an intermittent short in the detector system wiring. Such shorts may be caused by a loose wire that occasionally touches a nearby terminal, a frayed wire brushing against a structure, or a sensing element rubbing against a structural member long enough to wear through the insulation.
notes.choices:
A) A failed fire bottle squib
B) Low container pressure
C) Moisture, which always causes such alarms
D) An intermittent short in the detector system wiring
notes.choicesExplained: A: the squib is in the extinguishing system, not the detector. B: that gives a bottle pressure indication, not a fire alarm. C: moisture seldom causes a false alarm.

notes.front: A steady fire warning shows with no fire. You disconnect the engine sensing loop from the control unit and the alarm stops. Where is the fault?
notes.back: B) In the disconnected sensing loop, possibly bent into contact with hot engine parts
notes.explanation: If the false alarm stops with the loop disconnected, the fault is in the loop; if no bent element is found, isolate sections around the loop.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 9, “Fire Detection System Troubleshooting”, p. 9-12
notes.evidence: Such false alarms can be most easily located by disconnecting the engine sensing loop connections from the control unit. If the false alarm ceases when the engine sensing loop is disconnected, the fault is in the disconnected sensing loop, which should be examined for areas that have been bent into contact with hot parts of the engine.
notes.choices:
A) In the control unit
B) In the disconnected sensing loop, possibly bent into contact with hot engine parts
C) In the flight-deck warning light
D) In the fire bottle discharge circuit
notes.choicesExplained: A: the alarm stopped when the loop was disconnected, pointing to the loop. C: the light worked normally when the loop was removed. D: that circuit plays no part in the warning.

notes.front: How can an intermittent short caused by a kink in a sensing element be located?
notes.back: By checking the element with an ohmmeter while tapping it in the suspected areas to produce the short.
notes.explanation: Kinks and sharp bends can make an internal wire short intermittently to the outer tubing.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 9, “Fire Detection System Troubleshooting”, p. 9-12
notes.evidence: 3. Kinks and sharp bends in the sensing element can cause an internal wire to short intermittently to the outer tubing. The fault can be located by checking the sensing element with an ohm meter while tapping the element in the suspected areas to produce the short.

notes.front: If moisture does cause a false fire alarm, how long does the warning last?
notes.back: Until the contamination is removed or boils away and the loop’s resistance returns to normal.
notes.explanation: The handbook says moisture seldom causes a false fire alarm.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 9, “Fire Detection System Troubleshooting”, p. 9-12
notes.evidence: Moisture in the detection system seldom causes a false fire alarm. If, however, moisture does cause an alarm, the warning persists until the contamination is removed or boils away, and the resistance of the loop returns to its normal value.

notes.front: Pressing the fire test switch gives no alarm on a two-wire continuous-loop system. How can loop continuity be checked?
notes.back: C) Open the loop and measure its resistance
notes.explanation: No test alarm can come from a bad switch, control unit, power, light or an open in the loop; a two-wire loop’s continuity is checked by opening it and measuring resistance.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 9, “Fire Detection System Troubleshooting”, p. 9-12
notes.evidence: When the test switch fails to provide an alarm, the continuity of a two-wire sensing loop can be determined by opening the loop and measuring the resistance. In a single-wire, continuousloop system, the center conductor should be grounded.
notes.choices:
A) Ground the centre conductor
B) Heat the loop with a torch
C) Open the loop and measure its resistance
D) Discharge a fire bottle to confirm
notes.choicesExplained: A: that applies to a single-wire system’s normal state. B: the handbook describes a resistance check. D: discharging agent does not test the detector.

notes.front: What are two items of regular fire extinguisher system maintenance?
notes.back: Any two of: servicing bottles, removing and refitting cartridges and discharge valves, leak-testing discharge tubing, wiring continuity tests.
notes.explanation: The handbook lists these as typical regular maintenance.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 9, “Fire Extinguisher System Maintenance Practices”, p. 9-12
notes.evidence: Regular maintenance of fire extinguisher systems typically includes such items as the inspection and servicing of fire extinguisher bottles (containers), removal and reinstallation of cartridge and discharge valves, testing of discharge tubing for leakage, and electrical wiring continuity tests.

notes.front: A new fire extinguisher container arrives with its cartridge and discharge valve separate. What does the handbook say to do before fitting it?
notes.back: B) Assemble the cartridge in the discharge valve and connect the valve to the container, usually with a swivel nut and packing ring gasket
notes.explanation: Most new containers come disassembled, so the cartridge and valve are assembled and connected before installation.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 9, “Fire Extinguisher System Maintenance Practices”, p. 9-13
notes.evidence: Most new extinguisher containers are supplied with their cartridge and discharge valve disassembled. Before installation on the aircraft, properly assemble the cartridge in the discharge valve and connect the valve to the container, usually by means of a swivel nut that tightens against a packing ring gasket.
notes.choices:
A) Fit the container and install the cartridge later in flight-ready state
B) Assemble the cartridge in the discharge valve and connect the valve to the container, usually with a swivel nut and packing ring gasket
C) Fit the cartridge from the old container
D) Return it: containers must arrive assembled
notes.choicesExplained: A: assembly comes before installation on the aircraft. C: a removed cartridge should not go in another valve. D: most new containers come disassembled.

notes.front: In the handbook’s transport example, how does the bottle pressure switch work?
notes.back: It is normally open and closes an indicating circuit when pressure drops from a leak or discharge.
notes.explanation: It gives flight-deck indications when bottle pressure decreases.
notes.source: FAA, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 9, “Boeing 777 Fire Extinguisher System”, p. 9-14
notes.evidence: The pressure switch gives flight deck indications when bottle pressure decreases. The switch monitors the pressure inside the bottle and is normally open. When the pressure decreases because of a leak or bottle discharge, the switch closes an indicating circuit.
